Tap a cell to see where that aroma comes from, choose a roast level to see which groups stand out, then fill in your own tasting sheet. Figure 1 The MeDili flavor wheel. The inner ring shows general groups, the outer ring specific aromas. MeDili coffee per the product description Roast level Aroma groups by origin at this roast level Faded cells on the wheel are aromas that barely stand out at the selected roast level. Defect aromas stay unchanged because they do not depend on roast level. How to read Smell, taste, then choose a group on the inner ring : sweet, fruity, nutty… Move out to the middle ring if you can tell more: cocoa or roasted nuts? Name an outer-ring aroma only when you are sure. If unsure, stopping at the inner ring is also right. Defect aromas sit at the bottom of the wheel. If you find one here, trace the fault back to the farm, fermentation tank, drying yard or warehouse. Four origins of aroma Where the aromas in your cup come from. Coffee tasters often group aromas by when they form. This grouping is for nose training, not exact chemistry: one aroma can come from several pathways. Enzymatic Formed as the cherry grows and ripens, already present in the bean. Light and quick to fade, most evident in light roasts. Examples: Potato, pea, cucumber, tea rose, coffee blossom, lemon, apricot, apple, honey. Sugar caramelization Sugars and amino acids react during roasting, most strongly at a medium roast: Maillard reactions and caramelization. Examples: Vanilla, butter, toast, caramel, dark chocolate, roasted almond, roasted peanut, roasted hazelnut, walnut. Dry distillation Fiber and chlorogenic acids heated for a long time, prominent in dark roasts: wood, spice, smoke. Examples: Cedar, clove, pepper, coriander seed, malt, pipe tobacco, roasted coffee. Defect aromas Not produced by good beans but by spoiled cherries, over-fermentation, dampness and mold, or old beans. They can appear at any roast level. Examples: Earthy, straw, fruit skin and pulp, leather, stewed meat, cigarette smoke, medicinal, rubber. Aroma list The same content as the wheel, easier to read on a phone. Where it needs a different reading, MeDili notes it in the “Read again” section right after. A chemistry refresher Brew time does not just decide strength. It decides which compounds come out. Polyphenols come out first. Bitter compounds come out last. The same coffee gives different cups depending on when you stop. 1 Chlorogenic acids (CGA) and the acids that create bright acidity come out first . Most are out by the time extraction yield reaches 14% . 2 Sugars and Maillard compounds come out in the middle (14–20%). The figure calls this the SCA's “ideal” range. 3 Bitter phenolics come out last (after 22%). Over-extraction only adds bitterness, not polyphenols. Chart: from one batch of coffee, which compounds come out first First out: acids, CGA, polyphenols. In the middle: sugars, Maillard compounds. Last out: bitter phenolics. Vertical axis: percentage of compounds that have left the coffee. Horizontal axis: extraction yield (EY) 0–25%. Four lines: CGA, sugars, bitter compounds and caffeine (dashed). Three cups: same dose, same water, different times 15 g of coffee, 250 ml of water. What changes is which compounds come out. 1 minute: under-extracted. 4 minutes: ideal per the SCA, balanced. 8 minutes: over-extracted. Each cup has three bars: CGA, caffeine, bitter compounds. One place name, many layers of meaning Di Linh is in Lâm Đồng province, on a plateau long tied to coffee growing. The Di Linh plateau lies at about 900–1,000 m, with a cool climate and distinct rainy and dry seasons. That is the setting in which growers, processors and roasters work together. Drying coffee among the hills. MeDili's beans come from four growing areas: Gia Bắc 2, Lộc Châu 3, Tân Nghĩa and Tà Hine, 17.7 ha in total, plus 50 ha of partner farms in Di Linh. The growing areas have been cultivated since 2010. The line MeDili focuses on most is Cà Sẻ Di Linh. A place name on a bag is just words. Behind it are the people who pick the cherries when they are ripe, the drying yards, the rainy seasons that come early or late. Tasting with curiosity When you drink a cup of coffee from Di Linh, start with two open questions. The first: what is in this cup? Strength, bitterness, a cocoa aroma, or a little ripe-fruit sweetness. The second: what can't be known by taste alone? Where the farm is, when the cherries were picked, how many days they were dried. Those things need the people who make the coffee to tell them. A good cup can take the drinker back to a place. The job of the people who make coffee is to keep that place alive, with many voices and many harvests. In love with coffee, in love with Di Linh. x: Coffee Knowledge Brewing 3-minute read The phin and the drip of time. Why a small tool creates a very Vietnamese moment of waiting. A phin, a few spoonfuls of coffee, a kettle of water just off the boil. Then everyone has to wait. The first drop falls into the cup after about a minute, and the whole brew takes four to five minutes. There is no button to make it faster. That wait is part of a Vietnamese cup of coffee. A purposeful flow Phin brewing is not just following a recipe. Water passes through the coffee slowly enough for the brewer to watch, smell and wait. Meanwhile, the water draws out the strength, bitterness, sweetness and aroma of the roasted beans. There is no single number for every coffee. Grind size, amount of coffee, water temperature and tamping pressure all affect one another: A finer grind makes the water flow more slowly, giving a stronger cup that turns harshly bitter more easily. Tamping harder also slows the water down. Cooler water draws out less flavor, giving a weaker, more sour cup. More coffee gives a denser cup, and the water also takes longer to pass through. So treat a recipe as a starting point. Change only one thing at a time, then taste again. To see why one grind step or a few degrees of water change the whole cup, try the Extraction Machine : choose phin, turn each dial and watch acids, sugars and bitter compounds leave the bean in turn. MeDili's starting phin recipe 20–25 g of medium-ground coffee, lightly tamped. Pour 20 ml of water at 92–95 °C and bloom for 30 seconds. Pour about 60–80 ml more and wait 4–5 minutes. If the cup is too bitter, grind a little coarser. If it is weak, grind finer or add a few grams of coffee. A slower way to taste While the coffee is still warm, take a small sip before adding ice or milk. Notice three things: The first aroma as you bring the cup to your nose. The feeling on the tip of your tongue: bitter, sour or sweet, strong or light. The taste that remains after you swallow: lingering or fading fast. Only then add what you like: sugar, condensed milk, ice. Since you tasted the black cup first, you will know how the milk changed the coffee. Brewing well doesn't mean every cup is the same. What's worth keeping is understanding why a small change makes a different cup. There is always time for a good cup of coffee. x: Coffee Knowledge Coffee Knowledge 2-minute read From the coffee cherry to flavor. A short map of the transformations behind a coffee bean. A coffee bean is actually a seed inside a ripe red cherry. From the moment the cherry is picked to the moment the bean drops into the grinder, it goes through many transformations, and each one leaves a trace in the cup. A figure to picture it: in MeDili's model, 100 kg of fresh cherries gives about 18 kg of green coffee, then about 14.4 kg of roasted coffee. Most of the cherry's weight is lost on the way from farm to roastery. Selective picking of ripe cherries. Processing is a language Natural, Honey and Washed are the names of three processing methods. They differ in which layers of the cherry are kept during drying. Natural: the whole cherry is dried. The bean sits in the fruit flesh for a long time, so the cup is usually sweet with strong ripe-fruit aromas. Honey: the skin is removed, part of the mucilage is kept, then the beans are dried. The cup is usually rounded and sweet. Washed: the skin is removed, the beans are fermented, the mucilage is washed off, and only then are they dried. The cup is usually clean with bright acidity. Natural: whole cherries drying on raised beds. Honey: beans still in their mucilage, drying on raised beds. Pulping: a machine separates the skin from the beans. A name is no substitute for tasting. The result also depends on the variety, the ripeness of the cherries and the drying conditions. Two lots both labeled Honey can still give two very different cups. See the five layers of the cherry and which one is removed at which step in Cherry Anatomy , or try the seven-station fermentation machine . Roasting is the moment of understanding the bean In the roasting drum, heat drives water out of the beans, turning them from pale to yellow and then brown. Sugars and amino acids react with each other (the Maillard reaction), while sugars caramelize. These reactions create the aroma, color and crispness of roasted beans. The roast level is the balance point between the bean's character and the intended brewing method. Water passes through the coffee in a phin and in an espresso machine in two different ways, so MeDili roasts separately for phin and for machines. Water is the final stage. It carries the compounds formed during roasting into the cup. So roasting and brewing are two consecutive chapters of the same story. Which compounds reach the cup first and which come later, you can see in the Extraction Machine . Roasting and brewing are two consecutive chapters. Two-indicator map Focus · Robusta Cà Sẻ Di Linh Cà Sẻ is a variety, not a bean shape or a grade. “Sẻ” (“sparrow”) is a folk name, not an official classification. Cà Sẻ, Robusta Sẻ, Ro Sẻ and small-bean Robusta all refer to the Robusta brought to Vietnam in the early 20th century and widely grown in the Central Highlands before the selected varieties of the WASI institute. The trees are propagated from seed, so the population is uneven: each tree has its own shape, cherries and yield. The name reflects the small beans, small cherries and compact canopy. An analysis of 126 samples in WASI's gene bank showed that most Vietnamese Robusta material belongs to the ER genetic group, from the Congo River basin. From 1976, WASI began breeding on a large scale; the lines TR4, TR9, TR11, then TR14 and TR15 gradually replaced Cà Sẻ thanks to their high yields and large beans. Cà Sẻ is rarely planted now, but it is the foundation material of Vietnamese Robusta and holds many genes adapted to drought, pests and diseases. MeDili's Cà Sẻ farm The Di Linh plateau sits at about 1,000 m; the Robusta grows at about 900–1,000 m. Farmed since 2010; the trees are 15 years old and cared for naturally. The cool climate ripens the cherries slowly: they are picked in several passes from November to early January, with at most 5% green cherries. MeDili's observation: old Cà Sẻ trees give a delicious cup, rich in caffeine. Seven signs of Cà Sẻ No graft scar at the base The trees grow from seed. Walk a row of 20 trees and you'll see different shapes, leaves and cherries. What the research says Most of it is observational research over many years: coffee drinkers have a lower risk, but that does not prove coffee is the cause. Coffee is a drink, not a medicine. Topic Overall findings Level of evidence Alertness 40–300 mg of caffeine reduces tiredness, increases alertness and speeds up reactions Trials Type 2 diabetes Regular drinking is linked to a lower risk; within usual amounts, the more you drink, the lower the risk Observation Liver Linked to a lower risk of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer Observation Parkinson's Caffeine is linked to a lower risk; decaffeinated coffee is not Observation Depression Linked to a lower risk, but this may disappear at 8 cups a day or more Observation Cardiovascular Filter coffee up to 6 cups a day is not linked to a higher risk. The lowest risk is at 3–5 cups Observation Cancer Not linked to an increased risk of developing or dying from cancer Observation Longevity 2–5 cups a day are linked to lower overall mortality Observation The “cups” in the studies are standard American cups, much lighter than a strong Robusta phin.
